Eye infections Fungal infections of the eye are less common than infec- tions with bacteria or viruses, but are usually severe and may lead to loss of vision. Diagnosis may be delayed due to a gradual onset of symptoms and empirical treatment with antibacterials. Patients with impaired host resistance such as diabetics or immunocompromised patients are par- ticularly at risk. The most common fungi causing eye in- fections are Aspergillus, Candida, and Fusarium; others include Blastomyces, Cryptococcus, and Sporothrix. Cor- neal infection (keratitis) occurs most frequently, but the or- bit, eyelids, lachrymal sacs, conjunctiva, sclera, and intra- ocular structures may also become infected. Infections of the orbit rarely occur spontaneously but are more common with systemic fungal infection or may spread from the ad- jacent paranasal sinus tissue, as seen in mucormycosis or aspergillosis.1,2 Ocular fungal infections are difficult to treat. Diagnosis may be delayed due to a gradual onset of symptoms and empirical treatment with topical antibacte- rials or corticosteroids. Topical natamycin is generally considered the drug of choice for fungal keratitis due to filamentous fungi, while topical amphotericin B is an al- ternative. Topical amphotericin B with or without topical flucytosine, is preferred for yeast infections. Azoles exhib- it a wide spectrum of activity and clotrimazole, flucona- zole, itraconazole, ketoconazole, and miconazole are all used topically. Topical antifungals are not well absorbed and infections extending into the eye require subconjunc- tival, intra-ocular, or systemic therapy. Systemic treatment may also be indicated when there is a poor response to top- ical agents, for fungal endophthalmitis, or for ocular man- ifestations of disseminated fungal disease. When systemic treatment is indicated intravenous amphotericin B is usu- ally given. Azoles may be given for less severe infections or as adjunctive therapy in severe infections.
